L23: ## Description
L24: This dataset provides a collection of Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM) data, insulin dose administration, meal ingestion counted in carbohydrate grams, steps, calories burned, heart rate, and sleep quality and quantity assessment acquired from 25 people with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM). CGM data was acquired by FreeStyle Libre 2 CGMs, and Fitbit Ionic smartwatches were used to obtain steps, calories, heart rate, and sleep data for at least 14 days.
L25: This dataset could be utilized to obtain glucose prediction models, hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia prediction models, and research on the relationships among sleep, CGM values, and the rest of the mentioned variables. This dataset could be used directly from the preprocessed version or customized from raw data.

L0@P0: IPN Progress Report 42-233 • May 15, 2023
L1@P0: Square-Root Formulas for Kalman Filter,
L2@P0: Information Filter, and RTS Smoother:
L3@P0: Links via Boomerang Prediction Residual
L4@P0: Toshio Michael Chin∗
L5@P0: ABSTRACT. — A self-contained derivation of several square-root filter and smoother formulas
L6@P0: is presented. The formulas include square-root versions of the Kalman filter,
L7@P0: Rauch-Tung-Striebel (RTS) smoother, and Dyer-McReynolds Covariance Smoother (DMCS),
L8@P0: along with the square-root information filter (SRIF). A stabilized version of the RTS smoother
L9@P0: is also included. While most of the presented formulas have been independently derived and
L10@P0: well documented, this presentation takes an unified approach through a random process named
L11@P0: boomerang prediction residual, which simplifies both the derivations and formulas.
L12@P0: I. Introduction
L13@P0: Since its first application to aerospace navigation and guidance in 1960s, the Kalman filter has
L14@P0: become a common numerical tool in a wide range of applications for tracking the state of a
L15@P0: dynamic system based on incomplete and noisy observations. From the beginning, algebraic
L16@P0: realizations of the filter algorithm played a key role in successful applications, as the legendary
L17@P0: invention of the square-root filter enabled onboard deployment for the Apollo missions [1].
L18@P0: The square-root version significantly reduces round-off errors from digitization that can cause
L19@P0: filter failure. While the principal formulations for the square-root Kalman filter had mostly
L20@P0: been established by the mid-1970s [2, 3, 4], research on the square-root algorithms continued
L21@P0: along with advances in computational technology, including dedicated hardware for Kalman
L22@P0: filters [5] and method for parallel and distributed computing [6]. More recently, Kalman filter
L23@P0: implementations can rely on highly optimized linear algebra software packages such as
L24@P0: LINPACK/LAPACK [7]. Use of the QR-factorization, in particular, is seen often in
L25@P0: square-root filter implementations [8, 9].
L26@P0: *Tracking Systems and Applications Section.
L27@P0: The research described in this publication was carried out by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of
L28@P0: Technology, under a contract with the National Aeronautics and Space Administration. © 2023 All rights reserved.
L29@P0-1: 1This note presents a set of square-root realizations for the Kalman filter as well as the
L30@P1: Rauch-Tung-Striebel (RTS) smoother [10], which produces the fixed-interval smoothing
L31@P1: estimates by retrospectively upgrading the Kalman filter results. Development here has been
L32@P1: motivated by applications to space geodetic data for terrestrial reference frame estimation
L33@P1: [11, 12] in which the variance estimates are susceptible to becoming negative due to digital
L34@P1: round-offs. Generally, the standard Kalman filter and RTS smoother formulas share a
L35@P1: weakness in preserving numerical positive semi-definiteness in their covariance matrix
L36@P1: estimates. Addressing such an algorithmic weakness is a focal point of this note. The
L37@P1: square-root Kalman filter algorithms presented here are not new and are well documented
L38@P1: [3, 13, 14]. The accompanying square-root RTS smoother algorithm, on the other hand,
L39@P1: appears to have a simpler algebraic form than the existing ones [15] due partly to a new
L40@P1: derivation presented here. The smoother works well in tandem with either the square-root
L41@P1: Kalman filter or the square-root information filter (SRIF) [16]. The filter and smoother
L42@P1: algorithms here can be executed using only the standard LAPACK/BLAS linear algebra
L43@P1: subroutines for the QR and Cholesky factorizations and for triangular matrix inversion and
L44@P1: multiplication. The presentation is intended for general filtering and smoothing problems
L45@P1: beyond the target applications.

L192@P3: A well-known weakness in these formulas is that subtractions of one covariance matrix from
L193@P3: another, which appear in (8) and (13), are vulnerable to digital round-offs that may make the
L194@P3: difference matrix non-definite, violating the fundamental characteristic of a covariance matrix
L195@P3: to be positive semi-definite and leading often to swift divergence from optimality.
L196@P3: III. Stabilized Forms
L197@P3: The covariance formulas (8, 13) can be altered into “stabilized forms” to replace the
L198@P3: numerically vulnerable covariance differences with quadratic terms. A stabilized form of RTS
L199@P3: covariance recursion (13), rare or absent in the literature, is presented here. Its derivation
L200@P3: depends on the introduction of a process labeled here as “the boomerang prediction residual,”
L201@P3: which reappears prominently in the square-root forms of the Kalman filter and RTS smoother
L202@P3: presented later.

The quality of data acquired through wearable sensors is generally lower than what medical-grade devices provide, and existing datasets have mainly been acquired in highly controlled clinical conditions.
